newsitem.title: USA: U.S. report upbraids Germany over Scientology.
newsitem.headline: U.S. report upbraids Germany over Scientology.

text.p: The United States took issue with Germany on Thursday for political, business and cultural discrimination against Scientology in a report that a senior U.S. official said reflected "serious concern" in Washington.
But in its annual human rights report for 1996, the State Department also said there had also been "some positive developments" in Bonn's treatment of the group.

In the report, one of 193 covering the whole world, the department said a "sharp debate" surrounded the activities in Germany of the Church of Scientology, which German officials have portrayed as a potential threat to the public.

The report said German members of the Los Angeles-based church "allege both government-condoned and societal harassment, including expulsion from (or denial of permission to join) a political party and loss of employment."

The survey noted that major German political parties excluded Scientologists from membership and that the state of Bavaria had begun to screen applicants for civil service positions for Scientology membership.
Businesses whose owners or executives are Scientologists may face boycotts and discrimination, sometimes with government approval, it said.
Artists had been prevented from performing or displaying their works because of membership in the church, it added.
Four previous reports have raised the issue of Scientology in Germany, but this year's covered it at much greater length, reflecting, officials said, the publicity it has received in the past year.

Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, who oversaw the report, told a news conference: "We have expressed our serious concern about discrimination against Scientologists in Germany, and we will continue to do so."

In Los Angeles, the president of the Church of Scientology International hailed the State Department report as "the most decisive condemnation of German human rights terrorism since the end of World War II."

Rev. Heber Jentzsch said in a statement that the report "strips the artificial veneer from German-style democracy. It exposes these people as having zero justification for their unscrupulous and outrageous hate campaign."

The report said, however, that "the past year has also seen some positive developments," including a finding by the interior ministry that there was insufficient evidence to justify surveillance of the group by security agencies.
U.S. officials stressed that Germany was a close U.S. ally with human rights practices broadly in line with those of other Western countries.

"In the great scheme of things in the world ... the problems in Germany are in no way comparable to problems in Iraq, and in Sudan, or in China, or in Iran, countries which have severe human rights problems," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. "Let's put things in perspective."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday that the United States planned to increase its focus in the future on religious rights, but did not name Germany as a violator.
U.S. officials sidestep the issue of whether Scientology is legally a religion but say the United States accords it religious rights.

Scientology is a religious philosophy founded in 1954 by American science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. Its adherents include such prominent U.S. show business figures as filmstars Tom Cruise and John Travolta and jazz pianist Chick Corea.

State Department officials have repeatedly criticised U.S. Scientologists and their Hollywood supporters for newspaper advertisements and statements comparing German treatment of the group to the Nazi persecution of the Jews.
Although the human rights report did not mention this aspect of the controversy, Burns again denounced the comparison on Thursday.
